results.title: Income inequality in the EU: General trends and policy implications | CEPR
results.content:
Title: Income inequality in the EU: General trends and policy implications | CEPR
# Income inequality in the EU: General trends and policy implications. Using income survey data, this column shows that that inequality among EU citizens is significantly lower than among US citizens, but slightly higher than in countries with established welfare models such as Australia and Japan. In comparison to the US, the EU is well-known to have lower inequality levels within its member states combined with higher levels of income inequality between them. Albeit imperfect, EU income survey data are a powerful source to monitor inequality trends.2 The main instrument is the Statistics on Income and Living Conditions (EU-SILC), an annual dataset that collects harmonised information on income and living conditions across EU countries and allows us to analyse EU-level income inequality trends. EU-level inequality in disposable incomes, as measured by the Gini coefficient, is slightly below the inequality observed in the most unequal member states such as Bulgaria and Lithuania (Figure 1). **Figure 1** Income inequality in the EU in comparison to the most equal (top) and most unequal (bottom) member states (Gini coefficient, disposable incomes). The international comparison illustrates that EU-level income inequality is slightly higher than in countries with established welfare models, such as Australia and Japan. Despite being the result of the aggregation of countries with heterogeneous income levels and within-country inequality, with Sweden and Bulgaria at the two extremes, disposable income inequality among EU individuals stands significantly lower than among US individuals (Figure 2). **Figure 2** Income inequality in the EU in comparison to other countries (Gini coefficient, disposable incomes). In 2018, around 80% of the EU inequality depended on within-country inequality while 20% could be attributed to income differences between EU member states (Figure 3). **Figure 3** EU inequality decomposition by country (Theil index, disposable incomes). **Figure 4** Between-country inequality in the EU and euro area (Theil index and Mean Logarithmic deviation, Disposable incomes). **Figure 5** Inequality in market, gross and disposable income in the EU and the US. On top of these policy areas, primarily in the remit of member states, EU-level inequality is influenced by EU income convergence and cohesion policies and by the wide range of EU Single Market and single currency rules and policies.

results.title: Top Income Adjustments and Inequality: An Investigation of the EU‐SILC
results.content: # Top Income Adjustments and Inequality: An Investigation of the EU‐SILC. This paper provides a novel assessment of how the World Inequality Database (WID) top income adjustment applied by Blanchet, Chancel, and Gethin (2021) to European Union Statistics on Income and Living Conditions (EU‐SILC) data for 26 countries over 2003–2017 for Distributional National Accounts purposes affects inequality in equivalized gross and disposable household income. results.title: Household size in Ireland: Stylised facts and cross country trends | ESRI
results.content: # Household size in Ireland: Stylised facts and cross country trends. This paper uses cross-country data to explore the trends in household size in Ireland and to place these trends in a European context. Using cross country data from the EU-SILC survey, the research presents a range of stylised facts regarding how Ireland differs from other countries and attempts to explore what might explain the variation. However, this appears to be strongly influenced by demographics, with high fertility rate, younger population and thus high share of households with children important factors in explaining the cross country trends. In terms of the change over time in household size, we find little association with time-varying economic factors but, again, a strong effect of aging and the proportion of households with children. © 2024 The Economic and Social Research Institute, Whitaker Square, Sir John Rogerson’s Quay, Dublin 2.
